questions.q: Why is 'just restore from backup' often the wrong first instinct after a bad deployment, per this lesson?
options: A restore rolls back every legitimate transaction since the backup, potentially discarding hours of real data to fix a much shorter-lived problem
SQL Server does not allow restoring a database once a deployment has run
Backups cannot be used to restore schema changes, only data
Restoring always takes longer than any other option
questions.explain: A full restore discards all transactions since the restore point — often far more data loss than the problem it's meant to fix.

questions.q: What is a rollback script, as described in this lesson?
options: A script that reverses exactly the change a deployment made, written and tested alongside the deployment script before it ships
A backup file taken automatically after every deployment
A script that restores the entire server to factory settings
An automatic feature that undoes any failed T-SQL statement
questions.explain: The rollback script is prepared and tested in advance, as part of the deployment process, not improvised after something breaks.

questions.q: Why does version control for database objects (Lesson 49) directly help with rollback?
options: The previous version of a changed object is already sitting in source control history, ready to restore rather than being lost
It automatically writes rollback scripts with no manual effort
It prevents deployments from ever failing
It has no connection to rollback at all
questions.explain: If a procedure's old version is in source control, restoring it as part of a rollback script is straightforward instead of requiring reconstruction from memory.

questions.q: According to this lesson, when is point-in-time restore genuinely the right tool?
options: Once it's confirmed that data was actually corrupted or lost — not as the reflexive first response to any bad deployment
As the first action taken for every deployment issue, without exception
Only when the transaction log has been disabled
Never — point-in-time restore should not be used for deployment issues
questions.explain: Point-in-time restore is a legitimate, real tool for actual data loss/corruption, but it's the second option after confirming a scripted rollback can't undo the damage.

questions.q: In the lesson's example, a deployment breaks a stored procedure's logic at 2:15pm with no data corruption, on a database that's been taking real transactions all day. What is the better first response?
options: Run the tested rollback script to restore the previous procedure version, rather than restoring from backup
Restore last night's full backup immediately
Take the database offline until the next scheduled maintenance window
Wait until end of day to address it
questions.explain: With no data loss involved, a tested rollback script reverses the specific broken change without discarding the day's legitimate transactions.
